title: Feature Pyramid Networks for Object Detection

problem.summary: Detecting objects at vastly different scales is hard: featurized image pyramids are accurate but too slow and memory-hungry for end-to-end training, while the single-scale feature maps used by Fast/Faster R-CNN sacrifice accuracy, especially on small objects.
statements: Recent deep detectors avoid pyramid representations because they are compute and memory intensive.
Featurizing every level of an image pyramid raises inference time considerably and makes end-to-end training infeasible in memory, so image pyramids are used only at test time.
The ConvNet's in-network feature hierarchy has large semantic gaps: high-resolution maps carry low-level features that hurt recognition.
Single-scale detectors such as Fast/Faster R-CNN underperform multi-scale detection, particularly for small objects.

evidence.quote: But recent deep learning object detectors have avoided pyramid representations, in part because they are compute and memory intensive.
Inference time increases considerably (e.g., by four times [11]), making this approach impractical for real applications.
if exploited, image pyramids are used only at test time [15, 11, 16, 35], which creates an inconsistency between train/test-time inference.
The high-resolution maps have low-level features that harm their representational capacity for object recognition.

background.summary: The paper builds on featurized image pyramids (SIFT/HOG era), region-based detectors (SPPnet, Fast/Faster R-CNN), and multi-layer feature combination methods (HyperNet, ION, U-Net, SSD), arguing that existing pyramidal architectures produce a single high-level map rather than predictions at every level.

relatedWork.name: SSD
relatedWork.relation: first attempt to reuse the ConvNet feature hierarchy as a pyramid, but starts high in the network and misses high-resolution maps
relatedWork.quote: The Single Shot Detector (SSD) [22] is one of the first attempts at using a ConvNet’s pyramidal feature hierarchy as if it were a featurized image pyramid

relatedWork.name: Fast R-CNN / Faster R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: main baselines; use single-scale features by default
relatedWork.quote: Fast and Faster R-CNN [11, 29] opt to not use featurized image pyramids under default settings.

relatedWork.name: SPPnet
relatedWork.relation: showed region-based detectors work on single-scale feature maps
relatedWork.quote: SPPnet [15] demonstrated that such region-based detectors could be applied much more efficiently on feature maps extracted on a single image scale.

relatedWork.name: HyperNet / ParseNet / ION
relatedWork.quote: Several other approaches (HyperNet [18], ParseNet [23], and ION [2]) concatenate features of multiple layers before computing predictions, which is equivalent to summing transformed features.

evidence.quote: All recent top entries in the ImageNet [33] and COCO [21] detection challenges use multi-scale testing on featurized image pyramids
Multi-scale detection, however, still performs better, especially for small objects.

solution.summary: FPN builds a feature pyramid inside a ConvNet by combining the bottom-up pathway with a top-down pathway and lateral connections, yielding semantically strong maps at all resolutions that are used for prediction at every level with shared heads.
solution.approach: Upsample coarser semantically strong maps, merge them with same-size bottom-up maps via 1x1 lateral convolutions plus addition, and attach shared prediction heads to each pyramid level.
components: Bottom-up pathway using ResNet stage outputs {C2, C3, C4, C5}
Lateral 1x1 convolutions followed by element-wise addition
3x3 convolution on each merged map with d = 256 channels
Single-scale anchors per level: areas {32^2..512^2} on {P2..P6}, 3 aspect ratios (15 anchors total)
Parameter-shared RPN and Fast R-CNN heads across levels, with a light 2-fc head

evidence.quote: we rely on an architecture that combines low-resolution, semantically strong features with high-resolution, semantically weak features via a top-down pathway and lateral connections
The topdown pathway hallucinates higher resolution features by upsampling spatially coarser, but semantically stronger, feature maps from higher pyramid levels.
we assign anchors of a single scale to each level

experiments.summary: FPN is evaluated on COCO with RPN proposal recall (AR) and Fast/Faster R-CNN detection (AP), ablating top-down and lateral connections against single-scale ResNet baselines, plus mask proposal experiments following DeepMask/SharpMask.

evidence.quote: our FPN (Table 3(c)) is better than this strong baseline by 2.3 points AP and 3.8 points AP@0.5.
Placing FPN in RPN improves AR1k to 56.3 (Table 1 (c)), which is 8.0 points increase over the single-scale RPN baseline
On the test-dev set, our method increases over the existing best results by 0.5 points of AP (36.2 vs. 35.7) and 3.4 points of AP@0.5 (59.1 vs. 55.7).

limitations.summary: The authors deliberately keep the design simple (leaving better connection modules and heads unexplored), the ResNet-101 model was under-trained with the default schedule, and FPN does not yet incorporate several standard accuracy-boosting tricks.
items: More sophisticated connection blocks were only marginally better and were not studied further.
A stronger head architecture is expected to improve results but is out of scope.
The ResNet-101 model needed an extended learning-rate schedule to reach its reported AP.
Popular improvements (iterative regression, hard negative mining, context modeling, stronger augmentation) are not used.

evidence.quote: Designing better connection modules is not the focus of this paper, so we opt for the simple design described above.
We expect a stronger architecture of the head [30] will improve upon our results, which is beyond the focus of this paper.
We find that our ResNet-101 model in Table 5 is not sufficiently trained with the default learning rate schedule.

futureDirections.direction: Combine FPN with complementary accuracy improvements such as iterative regression, hard negative mining, context modeling and stronger data augmentation.
futureDirections.quote: These improvements are complementary to FPNs and should boost accuracy further.

futureDirections.direction: Adopt stronger head architectures on top of the feature pyramid.
futureDirections.quote: We expect a stronger architecture of the head [30] will improve upon our results, which is beyond the focus of this paper.

futureDirections.direction: Use FPN as a practical building block for future detection research and applications.
futureDirections.quote: We believe the efficiency and simplicity of our method will benefit future research and applications.

equations.name: anchor-to-level IoU labeling
equations.expr: positive if best IoU or IoU > 0.7; negative if IoU < 0.3

applications.detail: FPN is extended to generate object segment proposals following the DeepMask/SharpMask framework.
applications.quote: we use FPNs to generate segmentation proposals, following the DeepMask/SharpMask framework [27, 28].

applications.detail: FPN underpinned top results in COCO detection, instance segmentation and keypoint estimation tracks.
applications.quote: Recently, FPN has enabled new top results in all tracks of the COCO competition, including detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint estimation.

deploymentClaims: Runs at 6 FPS on a GPU as a practical multi-scale detection solution.
Inference takes 0.148 s/image (ResNet-50) and 0.172 s (ResNet-101) on a single NVIDIA M40 GPU, versus 0.32 s for the single-scale ResNet-50 baseline.
Mask proposal models run at 6 to 7 FPS, substantially faster than image-pyramid-based methods.

evidence.quote: our method can run at 6 FPS on a GPU and thus is a practical and accurate solution to multi-scale object detection.
Our method introduces small extra cost by the extra layers in the FPN, but has a lighter weight head.
